info.title: HighTech Store API
info.description:
The API behind HighTech Store: a PC hardware shop with a compatibility-checked PC builder, cart and checkout, payments
with idempotent webhooks, refunds, reconciliation and an admin area.

Every address below is relative to `/api`. Requests and answers are JSON (`Accept: application/json`).

## Logging in

The API uses a **cookie session** (Laravel Sanctum's SPA mode), not tokens. A browser on the shop's own website does all
of this by itself; another client has to keep cookies and follow three steps:

1. `GET /sanctum/csrf-cookie` (note: not under `/api`). It sets two cookies: the session and `XSRF-TOKEN`.
2. `POST /api/auth/login` with the email and password.
3. Send the cookies with every later request.

Every request that changes something (`POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`) must also carry the header `X-XSRF-TOKEN`, holding the
URL-decoded value of the `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie. Without it the answer is `419`. Requests are treated as logged-in only when
their `Origin` or `Referer` is the shop's own website.

Endpoints marked with a lock need a logged-in user. Where a **permission** is named, the user's role must hold it:
customers have none of them, staff hold the day-to-day ones, admins hold all.

## Money

Money is never a decimal. An amount is a whole number of **sen** (RM 1 = 100 sen) and is returned as an object:

```json
{ "amount": 119900, "currency": "MYR", "formatted": "RM 1,199.00" }
```

Amounts sent to the API (a product's price, a refund) are whole numbers of sen too. Prices, totals, discounts and
shipping are always worked out by the server from its own data: nothing a client sends can change what an order costs.

## Identifiers

Catalog records (products, categories, brands) have whole-number ids, and products are also addressed by `slug`. Orders,
payments, refunds and saved builds have 26-character ids (ULIDs) that cannot be guessed or counted. An order also has a
number meant for people, such as `ORD-2026-00018`.

## Errors

Every error has the same shape. `errors` is present only when what was sent failed validation, with one list of
messages per field:

```json
{
  "message": "Graphics Card X is out of stock.",
  "errors": { "cart": ["Graphics Card X is out of stock."] }
}
```

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `401` | Not logged in |
| `403` | Logged in, but not allowed to do this (someone else's order, or a missing permission) |
| `404` | No such address or record. Another customer's record also answers `404` or `403`, never its contents |
| `405` | The address exists but not for this method |
| `419` | The session or its `X-XSRF-TOKEN` expired: fetch `/sanctum/csrf-cookie` again |
| `422` | What was sent is not acceptable; see `errors` |
| `429` | Too many requests; the `Retry-After` header says how many seconds to wait |
| `500`, `503` | A problem on the server. The answer never contains internal details |

## Lists

Lists are paged with `page` and `per_page`. The answer has the rows in `data`, and `meta` (`current_page`, `last_page`,
`per_page`, `total`) and `links` (`first`, `last`, `prev`, `next`) to move through them.

## Placing an order safely

`POST /checkout` accepts an `Idempotency-Key` header (8 to 64 letters, digits, `-` or `_`). Sending the same key again,
for example after a timeout, returns the order that was already created (`200`) instead of making a second one (`201`).

## Payments and webhooks

An order is paid on the payment company's own page: `POST /orders/{order}/payments` returns the `checkout_url` to send
the customer to. The company then tells the shop what happened by calling `POST /webhooks/{provider}`. That call is the
only thing that marks an order paid; the page the customer returns to is never trusted.

A webhook is accepted only with a valid signature: a header holding `t=<unix time>,v1=<signature>`, where the
signature is HMAC-SHA256 of `<unix time>.<raw body>` with a secret shared between the shop and the company, and the
time is at most five minutes old. Each event is processed once: a repeated delivery is answered `200` with
`{"status": "duplicate"}` and changes nothing.

The built-in gateway is **FakePay**, a simulator for development and demos (its header is `x-fakepay-signature`). It is
switched off when the shop runs in production mode.

200.description: Understood. `status` says what was done: `processed`, `duplicate`, `ignored`, `amount_mismatch` or `late_payment`.

401.description: The signature is missing, wrong or too old.

400.description: The signature is valid but the body could not be understood.

429.description: Too many requests. The `Retry-After` header says how many seconds to wait.

session.description: The session cookie set by logging in. See "Logging in" above: requests that change something also need the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header.
session.name: pc-custom-store-session

AddBuildToCartRequest.description:
Adds a PC to the cart from EITHER a saved build (`build_id`) OR the parts currently in the builder (`items`).
Either way the server re-validates the build; nothing about it is taken on trust.
AddBuildToCartRequest.title: AddBuildToCartRequest

quantity.description: The exact limits (and the stock check) are enforced by CartService; this only checks the shape.

anyOf.description: The newest payment attempt (payments are loaded newest first), so the page knows what to show and whether to wait.

refund_pending.description: Money arrived that the order could not use (it had been cancelled): it will be refunded.

timeline.description: The order's story, oldest first: placed, paid, packed, shipped...

transactions.description: The raw payload the gateway sent is deliberately left out: the diary says what happened, not what was posted.

restock.description: Leave out to let the system decide: goods go back on the shelf only if the order never shipped.

BuildPriority.description: What matters most to the customer when two builds both fit the budget.
BuildPriority.title: BuildPriority

BuildPurpose.description: What the PC is for. It decides where the money goes: a gaming PC spends on graphics, an office PC needs none.
BuildPurpose.title: BuildPurpose

source.description: Who chose the parts: the shop's fixed rules, or an AI service whose choice then passed the shop's checks.

reasons.description: Why each part, in builder order.

BuildSelectionRequest.description: Shared rules for a list of selected parts: `items: [{slot, product_id, quantity}]`.
BuildSelectionRequest.title: BuildSelectionRequest

BuilderSlot.description: The PC-builder slots, in the order they appear on screen. A category joins the builder through categories.builder_slot (a database value), so which products fill a slot is data, not code.
BuilderSlot.title: BuilderSlot

in_stock.description: What a customer may know about stock: whether it can be bought, and a "low stock" warning.

inventory.description: Exact quantities are only included for staff who manage inventory.

params.description: The rule's own settings, by name (for example the spare power a PSU must have).

slots.description: The builder slots this rule looks at.

CouponRequest.description: Creating and editing a coupon. Money is in sen; a percentage is in basis points (1000 = 10%).

max_discount_amount.description: Only a percentage coupon needs a cap on how much it can take off.

CouponRequest.title: CouponRequest

value.description: percent: basis points (1000 = 10%). fixed: sen. `value_display` is the same thing in words.

reason.description: in sen, like every amount in this API

anyOf.description: The newest payment attempt (payments are loaded newest first), so the page knows what to show and whether to wait.

refund_pending.description: Money arrived that the order could not use (it had been cancelled): it will be refunded.

timeline.description: The order's story, oldest first: placed, paid, packed, shipped...

OrderStatus.description: Where the ORDER is in its life: from waiting for payment to delivered. Whether the money has arrived is a separate thing (PaymentStatus), so the two can never be confused.
OrderStatus.title: OrderStatus

checkout_url.description: Only an attempt that is still open has a page to go to.

PaymentStatus.description: What is happening to the MONEY for an order. Independent of the order's own status.
PaymentStatus.title: PaymentStatus

parts.description: In builder order (CPU, motherboard, RAM, ...), not the order the rows were inserted.

PlaceOrderRequest.description:
Only choices are accepted here: which address, which coupon code, an optional note. There is deliberately no
field for a price or a total. They are calculated by the server and anything extra the browser sends is ignored.
PlaceOrderRequest.title: PlaceOrderRequest

in_stock.description: What a customer may know about stock: whether it can be bought, and a "low stock" warning.

inventory.description: Exact quantities are only included for staff who manage inventory.

ProductRequest.description: Rules shared by creating and updating a product. Amounts are integer sen (RM 1.00 = 100).

specs.description: Per-category validation of the specs happens in SpecificationValidator.

ProductRequest.title: ProductRequest

in_stock.description: What a customer may know about stock: whether it can be bought, and a "low stock" warning.

inventory.description: Exact quantities are only included for staff who manage inventory.

specifications.description: Labels, units and order come from spec_definitions, so the frontend never hardcodes them.

RecommendBuildRequest.description: "Suggest a PC for me": a budget and what the PC is for. Everything else has a sensible default.

budget.description: In sen, like every amount: 400000 is RM 4,000.00.

games.description: Titles the customer plays. Only an AI recommender reads them, as a hint; plain words only.

order.description: For the staff queue: which order and customer this is about (load `order.user` first).

SaveBuildRequest.title: SaveBuildRequest

SpecType.title: SpecType

TargetResolution.title: TargetResolution
